title: Τοξότης καὶ λέων
part: The Archer and the Lion (Chambry 338 · Perry 340)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 338 (= Perry 340). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀνῆλθέ τις εἰς ὄρος τοξότης ἔμπειρος κυνηγῆσαι.
sentences.tr: Anēlthe tis eis oros toxotēs empeiros kynēgēsai.
sentences.l: A certain archer, an experienced one, went up onto a mountain to hunt.
sentences.i: An experienced archer went up a mountain to hunt.
sentences.n: κυνηγῆσαι is best taken as an infinitive of purpose after the verb of motion — 'went up to hunt'; it could also be construed with ἔμπειρος, 'skilled at hunting'. Ἀνῆλθέ carries a second accent thrown back on it by the enclitic τις that follows.

sentences.t: Πάντα δὲ τὰ ζῷα ἔφυγον, λέων δὲ μόνος προεκαλεῖτο αὐτὸν πρὸς μάχην.
sentences.tr: Panta de ta zōia ephygon, leōn de monos proekaleito auton pros machēn.
sentences.l: And all the animals fled, but a lion alone kept challenging him to battle.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ βέλος πέμψας καὶ τὸν λέοντα βαλὼν εἶπεν· « Ἰδὲ τὸν ἐμὸν ἄγγελον οἷός ἐστιν, καὶ δὴ τότε ἐπέρχομαί σοι κἀγώ. »
sentences.tr: Ho de belos pempsas kai ton leonta balōn eipen· « Ide ton emon angelon hoios estin, kai dē tote eperchomai soi kagō. »
sentences.l: And he, having sent an arrow and having struck the lion, said: « See my messenger, what sort he is, and then indeed I too come upon you. »
sentences.i: And he shot an arrow, hit the lion, and said: « See what sort my messenger is, and then I too shall be upon you. »
sentences.n: τὸν ἐμὸν ἄγγελον is pulled out of the indirect question and made the object of Ἰδέ — 'see my messenger, what sort he is' for 'see what sort my messenger is'. Greek does this constantly and the literal line keeps the order. ἐπέρχομαι is a present used of what is still to come, as English says 'then I am coming for you'. κἀγώ is καὶ ἐγώ by crasis.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ λέων βληθεὶς ὥρμησε φεύγειν.
sentences.tr: Ho de leōn blētheis hōrmēse pheugein.
sentences.l: And the lion, having been struck, set off to flee.

sentences.t: Ἀλώπεκος δὲ τούτῳ θαρρεῖν καὶ μὴ φεύγειν λεγούσης, ἔφη ὁ λέων· « Οὐδαμῶς με πλανήσεις· ὅπου γὰρ τοιοῦτον πικρὸν ἄγγελον ἔχει, ἐὰν αὐτὸς ἐπέλθῃ μοι, τί ποιήσω ; »
sentences.tr: Alōpekos de toutōi tharrein kai mē pheugein legousēs, ephē ho leōn· « Oudamōs me planēseis· hopou gar toiouton pikron angelon echei, ean autos epelthēi moi, ti poiēsō ; »
sentences.l: And a fox telling him to be of good courage and not to flee, the lion said: « You will in no way mislead me; for seeing that he has so bitter a messenger, if he himself comes upon me, what shall I do? »
sentences.i: But when a fox told him to take heart and not to run, the lion said: « You will not lead me astray in the least. Seeing that his messenger is as bitter as that, what shall I do if he comes at me himself? »
sentences.n: λέγω with the dative of the person and an infinitive is to bid or tell someone to do a thing, and the whole stands in a genitive absolute. ὅπου here is causal rather than local, 'seeing that', and its subject is the archer, left unexpressed. πικρός of a weapon is 'sharp, biting'; the bitterness of the messenger is the point of the lion's answer.

sentences.t: Ὅτι ἐκ τῆς ἀρχῆς τὰ τέλη δεῖ προσκοπῆσαι καὶ τότε δὴ λοιπὸν ἑαυτοὺς περισῴζειν.
sentences.tr: Hoti ek tēs archēs ta telē dei proskopēsai kai tote dē loipon heautous perisōizein.
sentences.l: That from the beginning one must look ahead to the ends, and then indeed thereafter keep oneself safe.
sentences.i: The story shows that one must look from the outset to how things will end, and only then set about keeping oneself safe.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, which begins simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. ἀρχή here is the beginning, set against τὰ τέλη, the outcomes; the same word can mean 'office', as at fable 236, and the contrast fixes the sense. δεῖ takes the infinitive with an unexpressed accusative subject, to which ἑαυτούς answers reflexively.
